shots.title: Households 65+ with $1 million or more
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: There are about forty million American households headed by someone sixty-five or older. {p} How many of them have a million dollars? {pp} According to the Federal Reserve's newest survey, counting everything they own, about thirty-two percent. Roughly one in three. {p} But that number changes a lot depending on what you count. {p} If you leave out the house, it drops to about twenty-three percent. {p} Count only savings and investments, and it's about eighteen percent. {p} And in retirement accounts alone, like 401(k)s and IRAs, only about eleven percent.

So is the million-dollar retiree common, or rare? {p} The honest answer is: both, depending on the question. {pp} In this video, we'll go through each definition, age group by age group, using the Fed's own public data. And at the end, we'll look at what a million dollars actually buys in retirement. {p} Why does this matter? Because millionaire headlines can make people feel behind, or falsely comfortable. Knowing which number you're looking at changes the whole picture. {p} <soft>As always, this is education, not financial advice.</soft>

shots.title: Four ways to count $1 million
shots.src: Federal Reserve SCF definitions: net worth, financial assets, quasi-liquid retirement accounts, home equity
shots.narration: First, the four ways to count. {p} One: net worth. Everything a household owns, including the home, minus everything it owes. {p} Two: net worth without the house. The same thing, but leaving out the equity in the home you live in. {p} Three: financial assets. Bank accounts, stocks, bonds, mutual funds and retirement accounts, but not real estate or businesses. {p} Four: retirement accounts only. 401(k)s, IRAs and similar plans. {pp} None of these include future Social Security checks or traditional pensions. So many retirees are better off than any of these numbers show.

Why does each definition matter? {p} Home equity is real wealth, but it's hard to spend without selling or borrowing against the house. {p} Financial assets can be spent, but there's a catch: money in a traditional 401(k) or IRA is taxed when you take it out. A million dollars in those accounts is not a million dollars after taxes. {pp} And retirement accounts are only one part of the picture for people who also have pensions, rental property or a small business.

items.text: House: real, but hard to spend

items.at: taxed when you take it out

shots.title: $1 million or more, counting everything
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: Let's start with the broadest measure: net worth, counting everything. {p} Across all American households, about twenty-two percent are worth a million dollars or more. {p} Among households aged fifty-five to sixty-four, about thirty-two percent. {p} Sixty-five to seventy-four, about thirty-one percent. {p} And seventy-five and older, about thirty-four percent. {p} For comparison, between forty-five and fifty-four it's about twenty-four percent, and under thirty-five, less than two percent. {pp} In total, that's roughly thirteen million households headed by someone sixty-five or older. {p} That surprises a lot of people. But it makes sense: these households have had decades for their homes, savings and investments to grow. {p} Many bought their homes decades ago, when prices were far lower. A house bought in the 1990s can be worth several times that today.

But a million dollars in net worth is not a million dollars in the bank. {p} For many of these households, a big piece of that million is the house they live in. You can't spend it without selling it, borrowing against it, or moving somewhere smaller. {pp} So let's take the house out.

items.at: not a million dollars in the bank

items.text: A big piece is the house

shots.title: $1 million or more, without the house
shots.sub: Net worth minus home equity · share of households, 2025
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: Without home equity, the share of millionaire households drops to about twenty-five percent at fifty-five to sixty-four, about twenty-three percent at sixty-five to seventy-four, and about twenty-three percent at seventy-five and older. {p} Still close to one in four. Notice the house matters most for the oldest households, who've had the longest to pay it off. {pp} But look at the middle household instead of the top. {p} Without the house, the typical household aged sixty-five or older is worth about a hundred and sixty thousand dollars. {p} At fifty-five to sixty-four, about a hundred and fifty thousand.

shots.title: Typical household, without the house
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: So the picture splits in two. {p} A large group, about one in four, has a million or more even without counting the home. {p} And the household right in the middle has about a hundred and sixty thousand. {pp} That's the gap a single average number hides. If you're somewhere in between, you're in very normal company. {p} Savings and investments tell a similar story: about nineteen percent of households at fifty-five to sixty-four, seventeen percent at sixty-five to seventy-four, and twenty percent at seventy-five and older have a million or more in financial assets.

shots.title: $1 million or more in retirement accounts
shots.sub: 401(k), IRA and similar plans · share of households, 2025
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: Now the strictest test: a million dollars in retirement accounts alone. {p} Across all ages, only about seven percent of households have that much in 401(k)s and IRAs. {p} At fifty-five to sixty-four, about twelve percent. {p} Sixty-five to seventy-four, about eleven and a half. {p} Seventy-five and older, about eleven. {pp} So the million-dollar 401(k) is real, but it's about one household in nine, even among people at or near retirement.

Why so few, when one in three is a millionaire overall? {p} Partly because 401(k)s only became common in the 1980s and 90s. Many of today's retirees spent part of their careers with traditional pensions instead. {p} And partly because much of their wealth sits elsewhere: in homes, businesses, and regular brokerage and bank accounts. {pp} That doesn't mean a 401(k) can't get you there. It means today's retirees, as a group, built their wealth in more than one place. For people now in their forties and fifties, who've had 401(k)s their whole careers, these numbers will probably look different.

shots.title: The typical millionaire household, 65+
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: So who are these millionaire households? {p} Among households aged sixty-five and older with a net worth of at least a million dollars, the one in the middle is worth about two point seven million. {p} About ninety-seven percent own their home, with about six hundred thousand dollars in home equity. {pp} For the typical one, the house is roughly a fifth of their wealth, not most of it.

shots.title: Millionaire households 65+: where the money is
shots.src: Nest Egg Atlas calculation from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances public data (survey weights) · 2025 dollars
shots.narration: Their typical retirement accounts hold about five hundred and thirty-two thousand dollars, and their typical financial assets, including those accounts, about one point three million. And only about thirty-five percent of these millionaires have a million or more in those accounts. {p} Their typical income is about a hundred and forty-three thousand dollars a year, from pensions, Social Security, investments and, for some, work. {pp} In other words, most millionaire retirees didn't get there with one giant 401(k). They got there with several pieces adding up. {p} Some in a 401(k) or IRA, some in a regular brokerage account, some in a business or rental property, plus Social Security, and often a pension. That's also why the averages in headlines can be so misleading.

shots.title: What $1 million buys, by the 4% rule
shots.src: 4% rule of thumb (Bengen, 1994): first-year withdrawal of 4% of savings, adjusted for inflation afterward · illustration, not advice
shots.narration: And what does a million dollars actually buy? {p} A common rule of thumb, the four percent rule, says you can withdraw about four percent in the first year, then adjust for inflation. {p} On a million dollars, that's about forty thousand dollars a year, or about thirty-three hundred a month, before taxes. {pp} Add Social Security on top, and for many households that's a comfortable retirement. {p} But it's a far cry from the image of a millionaire. A million dollars buys security, not luxury. {p} And remember, Social Security can add hundreds of thousands of dollars over a retirement, even though it's not counted in any of these numbers.

So, how many retirees really have a million dollars? {p} Counting everything: about one in three. {p} Without the house: about one in four. {p} In retirement accounts alone: about one in nine. {pp} If you're not in any of those groups, you're in the majority. And if you are, now you know exactly how rare your position is. {p} Tell me in the comments: which way of counting do you think is the fairest?

yt.title: How Many Retirees Actually Have $1 Million? (New Fed Data)
yt.description:
How many American retirees really have a million dollars? It depends on what you count. Using the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, we calculate the share of households aged 55–64, 65–74 and 75+ with $1 million or more: counting everything, without the house, in savings and investments, and in 401(k)s and IRAs alone. Plus a profile of the typical millionaire retiree household and what $1 million buys under the 4% rule.

Educational content, not financial advice.

Sources: Federal Reserve Board, 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, summary extract public data (our calculation with survey weights; all figures in 2025 dollars); Bengen (1994), 4% rule of thumb.
{music_credits}
Narration is AI-generated.
